kurz: What it costs to protect a portfolio against falling prices, calculated over 38 DAX years after premium and after tax.

bloecke.md:
A hedge does not make risk disappear. It exchanges risk for money, at a price that can be read off on the stock exchange. That a purchased put protects a portfolio is undisputed; it does so mechanically and reliably. What needs to be clarified, therefore, is what the protection costs, how often it pays out and whether the same result could be achieved more cheaply.

The basic case is the **protective put**. It consists of an existing equity portfolio and a purchased put on an index, with a strike price below the current index level. The shares remain in the portfolio, and the put pays the amount that is lost below the strike price.

bloecke.formel: Portfolio value at expiry = max(S_T, K) − P
bloecke.erklaerung: The put turns the linear price risk into a kinked line. Below K, the portfolio value falls no further; above K, the full upward movement is preserved. In both cases the premium has to be deducted; it is lost regardless of how the price develops.
variablen: index level on the expiry date
strike price of the put, that is, the floor
premium paid, per unit of the portfolio
bloecke.beispiel: Portfolio 100, put with K = 90 for P = 4.46. If the index falls to 40, the portfolio ends at 90 − 4.46 = 85.54, that is, at −14.46%. If it rises to 130, 130 − 4.46 = 125.54 remains. The break-even point is 104.46.

bloecke.md:
[[Put-call parity]] shows what you are doing in economic terms: `Share + put = call + cash amount K`. A hedged portfolio is the same as a call plus a fixed-term deposit. With the hedge, you are therefore not holding “shares with a safety net”. Without options, this position could only be replicated by continuous reallocation, that is, by selling when prices fall and buying more when they rise. The simplest alternative without options is to take part of the money out of the market. It reduces loss and return evenly and offers no floor. Every hedge has to be measured against this benchmark.

## Price of the hedge

The following prices are an illustrative calculation using Black-Scholes for an index without a dividend deduction (the DAX is a total return index and includes the dividends). The remaining term is one year and the interest rate 2.5%, in line with the ECB deposit facility rate since 16 September 2026. The assumed implied volatility is 18% at the money and rises by 2 points for every 10% decrease in the strike price. This is the skew typical of index options. For comparison, the VIX closed at 15.44 on 17 September 2026.

bloecke.titel: Price of a one-year put as a percentage of the portfolio value

bloecke.md: The table shows that the decision is less about protection or no protection than about the size of the excess. If the floor is raised from 90% to 95%, the worst-case loss falls by 3.7 percentage points (from 12.9% to 9.2%), because the higher premium takes back part of the five points. The premium rises by 45% in the process. The at-the-money put costs 5.92% a year. That is just over three quarters of the nominal return the DAX achieved from 1997 to 2025 (7.65% a year). In return, the put replaces the entire decline in every loss year. With the historical annual returns and this premium in every year, a portfolio with an at-the-money put bought anew each year would have achieved 8.93% a year over this period. Whether a hedge without an excess costs return therefore depends on the price of the protection and on the number and depth of the loss years.

A one-month put with a strike 10% below the current level costs 0.07% in the same model, or 0.80% annualised. That looks like a quarter of the price for the same protection. The protection is a different one, however, because each of these puts only limits the loss of its own month. Twelve months of −9% each add up to −67.8% without a single put paying out anything. The lower price corresponds to a different, much weaker benefit.

bloecke.md:
## The collar

The premium can be financed by also selling a call above the current price. This combination is called a **collar** and consists of three parts: shares, a purchased put and a sold call. It has a floor on the downside and a cap on the upside.

In the model above, the put at 90 costs exactly 4.46% if you apply the implied volatility of 25%, which is more realistic for long periods. The same amount is raised by a sold call with a strike price of 112, for which a lower implied volatility of just under 20% is assumed because of the skew. The net premium is therefore zero. This creates a **zero-cost collar** with a floor at −10% and a cap at +12.0%.

bloecke.titel: Zero-cost collar 90/112 on a portfolio of €100
bloecke.unter: Between 90 and 112, the position behaves like the share; outside this range the result is limited, to −€10 on the downside and +€12 on the upside.

bloecke.md: The collar costs no premium, but it does cost return. Of 38 DAX years since 1988, 22 were above +12.02%. The cap would therefore have limited the return in more than half of the years, while the floor would have helped in 7 years. For the premium of zero, you are thus selling upside opportunities that statistically occur more often than the losses you are hedging against.

## Four strategies over 38 DAX years

The following calculation applies four strategies to the historical calendar-year returns of the DAX total return index from 1988 to 2025. The protective put is bought anew every year with a strike price of 90%, at a constant premium of 4.46%. The collar corresponds to the one described above, with a floor at −10% and a cap at +12.02%. The fourth variant does without options entirely and holds 75% DAX and 25% money market at 2.5%.

bloecke.titel: Growth of €100 from the end of 1987 (logarithmic scale)
bloecke.unter: At the end, the put hedge ends up with a fifth less wealth and the collar with more than two thirds less, even though both lost considerably less in the crisis years 2002 and 2008.

bloecke.titel: Result 1988-2025, illustrative calculation based on historical annual DAX returns

bloecke.md:
The put fulfilled its purpose. The worst year improves from −43.9% to −14.5%, and the largest decline from −58% to −36%. The price paid was 0.67 percentage points of return a year and around a fifth of the final wealth.

An important figure is the tipping point, that is, the premium at which the hedge would have cost exactly nothing. Over all 38 years, this **break-even premium** is 3.79%. The value is mainly a consequence of the two crisis years 2002 and 2008 and is not a fixed quantity.

- From 1988 to 1999 (DAX +17.55% p.a.), the break-even premium was 1.38%. Any realistic premium would have produced a loss.
- From 2000 to 2011 (DAX −1.37% p.a.), it was 8.93%. In this period, almost any hedge would have paid off.
- From 2012 to 2025 (DAX +10.70% p.a.), it was 0.97%. The hedge caused practically nothing but costs.

The illustrative calculation assumes the same premium of 4.46% over all 38 years. In practice, implied volatility rises precisely when you want the protection. In autumn 2008 the VIX closed at 80.86, and in March 2020 at 82.69. At 40% implied volatility, the same put costs 9.54% instead of 4.46%. The calculation above therefore tends to make the hedge look too favourable rather than too unfavourable.

## Structural costs of hedging

The price of an option contains the expected payout under the risk-neutral measure. The payout expected under real-world probabilities is smaller, because shares rise on average. Under a distribution with an expected return of 7% and volatility of 20%, the one-year 90 put has an expected payout of 2.05%. It cost 2.89% in a calm market and 4.46% on the long-term average. The values of 2.05% and 2.89% are both based on volatility of 20%. The gap between them therefore arises from the higher expected return of shares compared with the interest rate, that is, from the equity risk premium. The gap between 2.89% and 4.46% is the volatility risk premium, which the buyer of protection pays and the option writer receives. That implied volatility is on average above the volatility later realised is one of the best-documented findings of options research. Systematic hedging is therefore a business with a negative expected value. You buy it as protection against a specific risk that you cannot bear, and not for the return.

Gains from the put are income from derivative transactions (Termingeschäfte) under Section 20(2) sentence 1 no. 3 EStG (Income Tax Act) and are taxed immediately at 26.375%: 25% flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) plus solidarity surcharge (Section 32d(1) EStG), and 27.82% or 27.995% with church tax. The price loss in the portfolio, on the other hand, is only a book loss and is not available for offsetting. If the shares are sold, the loss goes into the **share loss pot** (Aktien-Verlusttopf) under Section 20(6) sentence 4 EStG. Losses in this pot can only be offset against gains on shares, not against the gain from the put. With an equity ETF, the loss does go into the general pot, but it is reduced by 30% through the partial exemption (Teilfreistellung) under Section 20(1) InvStG (Investment Tax Act). At least the former €20,000 limit for losses from derivative transactions was abolished without replacement by the Annual Tax Act 2024 (Jahressteuergesetz) of 2 December 2024 (Section 52(28) EStG). Not tax advice; legal position as of September 2026.

bloecke.titel: DAX portfolio of €100,000 in 2008 with a hedge
bloecke.unter: Before tax, the put limits the loss to 14.5%; after flat-rate withholding tax on the hedging gain less the €1,000 saver's allowance, the loss is 21.0%.

bloecke.md:
## Basis risk

On Eurex, index options are liquid, whereas options on individual ETFs practically are not. Investors who hold a global portfolio and hedge it with DAX or EURO STOXX puts are hedging something other than what they own. Since 1988, the annual returns of the DAX and the MSCI World in euros have had a correlation of 0.87, which is high but not perfect. In 2018 the DAX lost 18.3%, the MSCI World in euros only 4.1%. The put would have paid out even though there was nothing to rescue in the portfolio. In 2022 the MSCI World fell by 12.8%, more than the DAX, which fell by 12.3%. The put would have paid 2.3%, while the portfolio was down 12.8%. The hedge thus becomes an additional bet on the difference between two markets.

In addition, there is the question of contract size. A EURO STOXX 50 contract is based on €10 per index point. The portfolio must therefore be large enough for a whole number of contracts to match the portfolio size. One advantage is that these index options are European-style and cash-settled, so there is no early assignment with them.

bloecke.md:
- With a fixed date and a fixed sum, for example when the money is needed in 14 months to buy a house, a loss is real and cannot be sat out.
- A concentrated position with a lock-up period, for example employee shares, may not be sold before the holding period ends.
- A sale would crystallise large unrealised price gains and make them taxable. The put bridges the time until a sale makes sense.
- With a loan-financed position that faces the threat of a margin call, the put protects your ability to act as well as your assets.

In all other cases, if you cannot stand the fluctuations, the equity allocation is too high, and additional options change nothing about that.

mitnehmen: A protective put exchanges price risk for a premium; that it protects is settled, and the only open questions are the price and the size of the excess.
Over 38 DAX years, the break-even premium was 3.79%, but between 0.97% and 8.93% depending on the sub-period. Whether a hedge pays off only becomes apparent in hindsight.
Zero-cost collars cost no premium but do cost return, because the cap limited the return in 22 of 38 years, while the floor helped in 7.
Because of the volatility risk premium, systematic hedging costs money in expectation; it serves as insurance and not as a means of increasing return.
In Germany, the hedging gain is taxed immediately at 26.375%, while the portfolio loss exists only on paper. This shifts the effective floor noticeably lower.

begriffe.text: Share or fund position with a purchased put whose strike price is below the current price. The loss is limited to the price minus the strike price plus the premium; the upward movement is preserved.
Share position with a purchased put as the floor and a sold call as the cap. In a zero-cost collar, the call premium fully finances the put; the price paid is the capped upward movement.
The annual hedging premium at which a hedged strategy achieves exactly the same final return over a period as the unhedged one. It can only be determined in hindsight.
Risk arising from the difference between the underlying of the hedge and the assets held. It turns a hedge into a separate bet on the relative performance of two markets.
Systematic premium of implied volatility over the volatility later realised. Because of this premium, purchased protection costs more in expectation than it pays out.
